The Common reed bunting (Emberiza schoeniclus) is a small passerine that inhabits dense reed beds and marshy fringes across the Palearctic. Recent respirometry trials on captive individuals measured the species' maximum basal metabolic rate, recording a value of 54 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 54 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when the birds were maintained at an ambient temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This relatively elevated oxygen consumption, measured under thermoneutral conditions, likely reflects the high energetic demands of active thermoregulation and foraging in a structurally complex and often cold wetland environment. Within the genus Emberiza, such a metabolic rate is consistent with values reported for related species of similar body mass, although intraspecific variation related to seasonal fattening and molt has not yet been fully characterized. Newly hatched chicks emerge from the egg at a very modest size, with a wet weight at birth of only 1.7 grams [Wwb = 1.7 grams]. This low neonatal mass is typical of altricial songbirds, which require intensive parental brooding and provisioning to achieve rapid somatic growth in the first days post-hatching.

The developmental trajectory of the reed bunting is tightly constrained by thermal conditions during the incubation and early nestling periods. When eggs are incubated at a constant temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C], the age at birth—defined here as the moment of hatching—is approximately 13 days [ab = approximately 13 days]. This incubation period is somewhat shorter than that observed in some temperate congeners, potentially reflecting an adaptive acceleration of embryonic development in response to the brief and unpredictable summer window typical of northern breeding latitudes. The initial wet weight of the freshly laid egg, which represents the starting point for all subsequent growth, has been recorded at 2.345 grams [Ww0 = 2.345 grams]. Dry mass measurements of the yolk and albumen components suggest that this initial capital is efficiently converted into embryonic tissues during the 13-day incubation span. Once hatched, the altricial nestlings are entirely dependent on their parents for heat and food, and their growth rate is strongly influenced by the ambient temperature of the nest microclimate.

Under the thermal conditions that characterize the active metabolic and breeding period of this species, a series of key life-history milestones unfold at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. The time since birth at fledging, when the young bird achieves its first sustained flight and departs the nest, is 11.5 days [tx = 11.5 days]. at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]This rapid fledging period is notably brief compared to other passerines of similar adult size, suggesting a strong selective pressure for early nest departure in the face of high predation risk within exposed reed habitats. In comparison, the attainment of sexual maturity occurs considerably later: the time since birth at puberty is 34.5 days after birth [tp = 34.5 days after birth] at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This interval between fledging and the onset of gonadal maturation underscores the energetic investment required to complete post-juvenile molt, build fat reserves, and acquire a breeding territory. The delay is typical of species in which males must establish and defend a high-quality song perch before attracting a mate.

Reproductive output in the Reed Bunting is best characterized by the combination of clutch size and the frequency of nesting attempts. Females typically lay a single clutch of 4 or 5 eggs per nesting attempt [N_R_i = 4 or 5 eggs per nesting attempt] and can produce up to 2 broods per year [F_R_i = up to 2 broods per year] under favorable conditions, translating into a maximum annual reproductive rate that is nonetheless constrained by the short breeding season. The time since birth at first brood, marking the age at which a young female initiates her first successful breeding event, has been documented at 365 days since birth [tR = 365 days since birth] at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This deferred reproduction is characteristic of migratory passerines that require their first full year to complete the cycle of physiological maturation, pre-breeding dispersal, and territory acquisition. In a comparative context, this age at first reproduction is consistent with that of other Emberiza species, although the reed bunting's dependence on ephemeral wetland habitats may introduce interannual variability linked to water level fluctuations.

Longevity data for the Common reed bunting are derived primarily from mark-recapture studies conducted across Western European ringing schemes, which indicate a maximum recorded lifespan of approximately 12.25 years [am = approximately 12.25 years] when birds are captured and monitored under field conditions averaging 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] during the active season. In terms of adult body size, there is a pronounced sexual size dimorphism in this species: the ultimate wet weight for females typically reaches 17.7 grams [Wwi = 17.7 grams], while males attain a slightly larger asymptotic mass of 19.7 grams [Wwi = 19.7 grams]. This difference likely reflects the selective advantages of larger body size in male-male competition for song perches and territories, whereas the smaller mass of females may reduce energetic costs during the demanding incubation period. The wet weight at emergence of a newly hatched chick of 1.7 grams [Wwb = 1.7 grams] is therefore only about 9 to 10 percent of the adult female mass, underscoring the immense growth trajectory that altricial nestlings must complete over the course of their brief nestling period.
